verdict.tagline: A grim border checkpoint where bureaucracy meets impossible moral choices.
for_you_if: you enjoy meticulous document inspection puzzles
you want branching narratives with multiple endings
you like managing moral dilemmas under pressure
not_for_you_if: you struggle with a harsh learning curve
you dislike strict monetary penalties for mistakes
you need a gentle, welcoming tutorial

cohorts.summary: Players check documents at a border checkpoint and manage family expenses, though the tutorial requires learning through a difficult struggle.

claims.claim: The game features a mechanic where players check documents like passports, permits, and rules at a border checkpoint, cross-referencing details such as names, dates, and photos to approve or deny entry.

citations.review_text:
Papers, Please is one of those games that sounds boring when you explain it, but somehow becomes really stressful and addictive when you actually play it.

On paper, you are just checking passports at a border booth. You look at names, dates, photos, stamps, permits, rules, and decide who gets in and who gets denied. That sounds simple, but the game slowly keeps adding new rules until your desk becomes a complete mess of documents, mistakes, pressure, and moral choices.

The best part is how the game makes you feel the weight of small decisions. Sometimes it is not just “is this passport valid?” Sometimes a person begs you to let them in. Someone wants to reunite with family. Someone looks suspicious. Someone offers a bribe. Someone gives you a sad story, and you have to decide whether helping them is worth risking your job or your family’s survival.

And that is what makes the game special. You are not playing a hero with a gun. You are just a tired worker trying to earn enough money for rent, food, heat, and medicine. Every mistake costs money, and at the end of the day your family still needs to survive. So even when you want to be kind, the game pushes you into thinking like the system wants you to think.

The gameplay is surprisingly tense. You start checking documents quickly, thinking you have everything under control, then suddenly you miss one tiny detail and get a citation. Wrong date. Wrong district. Missing seal. Different name. Expired permit. It makes you paranoid in a good way. After a while you start staring at every person like they are trying to trick you.

The art style is simple, but it fits perfectly. The gray colors, rough faces, cold music, and ugly little booth make the world feel oppressive. It is not a “beautiful” game in the normal sense, but it has a very strong identity. Everything feels uncomfortable on purpose.

My only warning is that it can get repetitive if you are not into this kind of gameplay. You are basically doing paperwork un…

Papers, Please
.
A great game with the cool mechanic of passport control!
.
Controls:
Mouse control
.
Mechanics and features:
We see a line of people who want to enter the country, press the speaker to call the next person in line, then check their passport, and then you will get a stamp "Denied" or "Approved"
Rocking music in the main menu.
Pay attention to the applicant's nationality.
After a workday, we're shown our salary, with rent and heating costs subtracted. The remaining money must be spent on our family. After completing a level, we're also shown our family's condition, including who's doing well and who's not.
The Inspector's Booth contains:
- Shutter
- Counter
- Rule Book
- Audio Transcript
- Bulletin Storage
- Time & Date

claims.claim: The tutorial is described as very bad, requiring players to learn by doing through a struggle with mechanics and a rule book.

citations.review_text: i thought the game would be better considering what ive heard but its honestly way too difficult, if you cant think quickly like me and or have adhd and cant remember every single detail about things you wont be able to beat this. easy mode doesnt even make it easier it just gives you more money. im not sure how im expected to remember every rule in the rule book and remember the names of every city ontop of having to do it quickly without messing up at all. i failed on the 2nd day.

Maybe this is what unemployed people play to find fulfillment in life, but man, I would rather work my 9-5 than play this game. The amount of effort and exhaustion that comes with learning this game might as well go into working an actual job.
I went in thinking this would be a fun "catch the discrepancies, lol fun fun yippie!" and not a "ok so no what you wanna do is check this with that and don't forget this rule and consult the manual and oh by the way your family of 12 is starving to death" like what in the world

The tutorial is also very bad. It was a struggle to learn exactly how to use certain mechanics even after reading the manual over and over and over again. You essentially have to learn by doing, which at that point you only get to admin 5 people before the next day.
It has a snowball effect where you barely learn one thing, and then the next day you're introduced to a new mechanic or something else, making yourself even more confused.
If I hadn't known the gist of this game and went in blind, I would have been totally lost

claims.claim: Reviewers mention that keyboard shortcuts for actions like stamping and inspecting help speed up the workflow.

citations.review_text:
If someone had described me the game, I never would've liked it. Now I've played it, it is brilliant. A bit tense and requires a lot focus, but super entertaining nonetheless. Great game overall, interface, music, graphics, story, and an overall atmosphere.  You can really live the dystopian 1984-ish, heartless experience through such a simply designed gameplay.

One little comment if I want to be very critical, keyboard shortcuts can be improved a bit, e.g. last unlocked shortcut (double click to investigate) I did not find this quite useful, I would've appreciated e.g. a shortcut that returns all papers to applicants in one click. But hey, that's minor.

This, for me, is a masterpiece of a game. KUDOS to the developers and anyone involved in the game.

GLORY TO ARSTOTZKA

Checking passports may seem boring, but the story, characters, rules, variations, and document types fill in the gaps. While it does get complex, having a rhythm speeds up the process tremendously. 

Having to make questionable decisions for the tokens is a part of the job. Real border agents get bribed and harassed too. It is not pretty, but it is true. 

The keyboard shortcuts (for the stamp and the inspection) massively speed up the process.

I experienced zero technical difficulties. No stuttering, freezing or crashing. The game just works.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that as the game progresses, criteria and rules become more complex, adding new documents, restrictions, and moral choices that clutter the workspace and increase tension.

citations.review_text: This is a dystopian game where you play as a border controll agent. You get to check all the necessary papers and grant or deny entry. The further along the game you get, the more complex the criteria becomes. The game is a great commentary on corruption, state control, terrorism, morailty and revolution. You get to make decisions on who enters and not, and you steer where the story will go as your decisions matter. Great game!

How does one evaluate a game that accomplishes everything it sets out to do even when those goals include being intentionally uncomfortable and tedious? 

By gamifying a dead-end job and adding difficulty via penalties, time pressure, awkward controls, and visual clutter, it invests you enough in success that the moral decisions that jeopardize that success have consequence. The bureaucracy isn't just the setting, it's an ingenious misdirection to trick the "player" into honestly empathizing with a historical situation that they've likely kept at a safe emotional distance. Typically, such empathy is the purview of literature, but there might not exist a tolerable book that could get us in this headspace. Gamers are accustomed to occasional difficult monotony.

As for those quotes around "player": it's no intolerable book, but it's still not fun and it's barely playing. I'm semi-confident it's not meant to be fun, or at least not any more fun than the curious novelty of a new job before it's just work. The engagement comes from the weight of the story, the artistry of the design, and that empathy. I cared enough that each time the sanction printer's sound cued unexpectedly, I felt genuine dejection.

I improved at reviewing documents quickly, at memorizing the exact spelling of fictional cities, at comparing meaningless strings of characters, not because it was gratifying, but because it granted me the freedom to make the decisions I wanted. Which is why I cannot fathom the sort of masochist or incurably bored person who would voluntarily play the included storyless "Endless" mode. But maybe I'm the weirdo, since if children and bar patrons have taught me anything, it's that people love spot-the-difference games. 

Even though many, maybe even most, people would not strictly-speaking enjoy the game, I think just about everyone could stand to benefit from experiencing it, and might in the process appreciate its sneaky beauty.

7/10

P.S. Papers, Please too…

A beautiful game that will stress you out. Each stamp of approval forces you to hold your breath and hope it's not another citation. New documents, restrictions, and moral choices keep piling onto your desk until the screen becomes a cluttered mess. Everything in the booth from the rulebook to the sound design comes together to paint a cruel, believable world. I only wish the rest of the game had that same level of polish, with cutscenes and an end-of-day screen that feel underdeveloped compared to the checkpoint. Still, the core gameplay is so tuned and cohesive that those complaints feel small. A cold, unforgettable masterpiece. Glory to Arstotzka.

Very interesting and unique game concept. What stands out the most is how realistically the game depicts the heaviness of living in Soviet Union like countries. There are a lot of interesting choices and characters, multiple endings, but there might be an issue with motivation to discover them all as the core gameplay loop is a bit tedious. claims.claim: Reviewers highlight that decisions involve moral dilemmas regarding whether to help individuals or follow rules to sustain the player's family.

citations.review_text: Great game, loads of endings to unlock, the moral dilemmas are very strong as well, overall great buy for $10.

Papers, Please is the only game where your greatest weapon is… a stamp.

You play as an immigration officer in the glorious nation of Arstotzka, where your job is simple: check documents, approve or deny entry, and try not to accidentally destroy someone’s life before lunch.

At first, it’s easy. Passport? Check. Photo matches? Cool. Stamp it.
Then the game slowly adds more rules until your desk looks like a conspiracy theorist’s bulletin board.

“Entry permit required.”
“Wait, now you need an ID card.”
“Actually, also check for discrepancies.”
“Also terrorists exist. Good luck.”

Suddenly you’re inspecting passports like a detective, comparing dates, cities, fingerprints, and questioning why someone is definitely lying about being 6’2”.

The real challenge isn’t just accuracy it’s survival. You get paid per correct decision, which means every mistake costs money. And money keeps your family alive. So now every stamp is basically a moral dilemma:

“Do I help this desperate person… or do I feed my family tonight?”

Also sometimes you’ll deny someone for missing paperwork and they’ll just stand there like, “Please…”
And you’re like, “I’m sorry, but your documents are incorrect.”
And then you feel like a villain for the next 10 minutes.

The atmosphere is bleak, the humor is dark, and the gameplay is weirdly addictive. You will become faster, colder, and disturbingly good at spotting fake documents.

10/10 Glory to Arstotzka. I have never feared paperwork more.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the game as progressively introducing new rules and mechanics over time, which increases the challenge.

citations.review_text:
The concept of Papers Please alone earns it a permanent seat in the conversation about what the medium can do. You play a border inspector in a grim fictional Soviet-bloc country, stamping documents and deciding who gets through. Somehow, that simple loop stays genuinely compelling far longer than it has any right to. Lucas Pope somehow built an entire moral and political framework out of a document checklist, which is either brilliant or absurd depending on how you look at it. 

The tension it generates is surprisingly real. The rules compound over time, the documents get more complex, and the human stories layered into the mechanical routine create genuine moments of conflict where following the rules and doing the right thing are not the same thing. For a game about paperwork it carries unexpected weight.

The humor is understated but consistent. There's something inherently ridiculous about the premise that the game never fully winks at, which makes it land better than it would if it was trying harder to be funny. The absurdity speaks for itself.

It does wear out eventually. The core loop hits its ceiling before the game hits its ending, and the final stretch requires a patience that not everyone will have for what is ultimately a more complex version of the same thing you've been doing for hours. Getting to the finish line is satisfying but the journey there has diminishing returns.

On PC it's a clean, precise experience that suits the game perfectly. On Steam Deck the interface gets fiddly enough that it adds friction to a game already built around careful attention to detail, so if you have the option to play on a desk with a mouse that's the right call.

Lucas Pope followed this up with Return of the Obra Dinn, which is on my wishlist nwo and worth looking up if you haven't already.
